newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican lawmaker urges peso, inflation flexibility.
newsitem.headline: Mexican lawmaker urges peso, inflation flexibility.

text.p: A top Mexican lawmaker, in charge of the Congressional Finance Committee, is pressing the central bank for more flexibility on peso and inflation policy so as not to stifle Mexico's growth prospects next year.

In an interview Tuesday, Francisco Suarez Davila, who heads the committee that oversees the budget and Banco de Mexico and is a powerful member of the the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), was adamant that growth must accelerate next year.

"From the point of view of the PRI, the imperative for the country is to grow," he said, adding that the economy should increase at least four percent next year, and if possible five percent. This year, it is expected to grow four percent.
He said he respected Banco de Mexico's anti-inflation mandate, but believed it should not go too far.

"There is a discussion going on here. I respect the position of Banco de Mexico to lower inflation as much as possible, but the Congress, public opinion and the government's position is that, fair enough, you have to moderate inflation, but not so much that the recovery is not as strong as it should be."

Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said this week inflation should fall to 15 percent next year from around 25 percent at year-end 1996. Banco de Mexico Governor Miguel Mancera said it should be around half this year's level, with gross domestic product growth of some four to five percent in 1997.

Suarez Davila said inflation next year should be in the 15-20 percent range, depending on other aspects of the 1997 budget due to be presented to Congress in mid-November. He agreed with Ortiz that the country could afford to run a one percent of GDP budget deficit next year.
Some economists have raised doubts about the recovery's potential, particularly because of the lingering strength of the exchange rate, which threatens to curb a strong trade surplus.

Suarez Davila agreed that the appreciation of the exchange rate against the dollar was threatening to limit Mexico's export strength, and he also suggested Banco de Mexico was using the peso as an anchor against inflation, a move he was at odds with.

"A yellow warning light is flashing and that light is saying that the exchange rate is appreciating in real terms, that it has appreciated this year more than 15 percent in real terms, chiefly because of reversible movements of short-term capital."

In 1994, Mexican financial authorities played down the overvalued peso, a decision that came back to haunt them when the government was forced into a devastating devaluation in December that year. Suarez Davila said it was important to prevent that happening again.
"Everyone is very happy because inflation is falling, but suddenly you get a peso slide, and you lose everything you have gained. That's what we have to avoid," he said.

He said to stop the peso overvaluing, the central bank should consider buying dollars to boost reserves. He also argued that maintaining a healthy balance of payments was more important than using the peso as a tool against inflation.

Suarez Davila, who is a Cambridge-educated former Finance Ministry undersecretary and Banco de Mexico official, said he would raise his doubts with Banco de Mexico officials when they discuss their first-half results in Congress shortly.
